idiom_name: discriminated union plus exhaustive switch with a never-check at the boundary
implementation_notes: The type system is the mechanism: model each source format as a member of a discriminated union with a literal tag, and switch (raw.kind) narrows automatically, with an assertNever final branch that makes the compiler reject any unhandled format - one artifact replacing the Translator interfaces and the registry's completeness invariant. Because types are erased at run time the same seam must validate: parse as unknown and refine with z.discriminatedUnion('kind', [...]) (or Ajv/io-ts), which is exactly the router the pattern calls for, and then map each validated member to the single canonical interface the rest of the program uses. A Map<string, (raw: unknown) => Canonical> is the pragmatic form when the tag space is data-driven rather than known at compile time, and stateful translator classes are justified only when a mapping needs injected collaborators.
pitfalls: as casts and any at the boundary defeat the narrowing the pattern relies on: parse to unknown, validate with a schema, and let inference carry the tag.
Structural typing checks only the members you mention and excess-property checks apply to object literals only, so runtime validation is still required even though the union looks closed.
JSON.parse returns any and silently loses precision beyond 2^53: canonical ids and money should be strings validated by the schema.
Record<string, Normalizer> lookups inherit Object.prototype members (constructor, toString), so use a Map, Object.create(null), or a literal-union kind so the tag space is closed.
